The [uncertainty article](isoformic-uncertainty.html) turns Salmon's inferential replicates into an uncertainty for every isoform and a confidence for every call.
This article asks the next questions: which isoforms are uncertain, why, and how far the replicates themselves can be trusted.
It looks at three things for every isoform:

- **how uncertain** its abundance is: the inferential relative variance (InfRV) [@swish] with 100 Gibbs draws;
- **how reliably** 30 draws measure that uncertainty: whether two independent sets of 30 draws put the isoform on different sides of the 0.5 cutoff that `add_uncertainty()` uses to call it uncertain (a *cutoff flip*), and how much the two estimates differ;
- **how stable** its TreeTerminus tree is [@treeterminus]: whether the transcripts of its tree change between trees built from 30 and from 100 draws.

and relates them to the transcript type and to molecular features of the isoform and its gene.

## The data

Three samples of the prostate ESRP2 knockdown of the uncertainty article (two controls and one knockdown; 12 million read pairs each) were quantified with Salmon 2.8.0 against GENCODE v49, with 100 Gibbs draws, and once more with 30.
Isoforms with at least 5 estimated reads in a sample are kept, and the measures are averaged over the samples where the isoform is expressed.
The features come from the annotation, the transcript sequences and the equivalence classes:

| Feature | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `reads` | estimated reads of the isoform |
| `tx_length`, `n_exons` | length and exons of the isoform |
| `isoforms_in_gene` | annotated isoforms of its gene |
| `gc` | GC content of the transcript sequence |
| `mane`, `tsl` | MANE Select tag; transcript support level |
| `unique_bp` | exonic bases no other isoform of the gene covers |
| `closest_bp` | exonic bases that differ from the most similar sibling (both directions) |
| `contained` | all its exonic bases are inside another isoform's |
| `nagnag` | an acceptor site three bases from an acceptor of another isoform (NAGNAG) |
| `near_acceptor`, `near_donor` | a splice site 1 to 30 bases from another isoform's |
| `unique_fraction` | share of its fragments compatible with it alone (equivalence classes) |

`data-raw/knockdown/isoform_features.R` computes everything; the tables used below ship with the package.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(isoformic)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

stability <- function(name) {
  read_parquet(fs::path_package("isoformic", "extdata", "knockdown", "stability", paste0(name, ".parquet")))
}
type_labels <- c(
  protein_coding = "protein coding",
  nonsense_mediated_decay = "NMD",
  retained_intron = "retained intron",
  protein_coding_CDS_not_defined = "CDS not defined",
  lncRNA = "lncRNA",
  other = "other",
  all = "all"
)
```

## By transcript type

```{r}
by_type <- stability("by_type")
by_type |>
  select(type, isoforms, median_reads, median_isoforms_in_gene, median_unique_fraction, median_inf_rv, cutoff_flip, tree_changed)
```

Three different pictures emerge.

- **Protein-coding isoforms are the most uncertain and the most reliably measured.** Their median InfRV is the highest (`r by_type$median_inf_rv[by_type$type == "protein_coding"]`): they belong to genes with many isoforms (median `r by_type$median_isoforms_in_gene[by_type$type == "protein_coding"]`) that share their exons, and half of them have no fragment of their own. But their InfRV is far above the cutoff, so 30 draws rarely put one on the other side (`r round(100 * by_type$cutoff_flip[by_type$type == "protein_coding"], 1)`% flip).
- **Retained-intron, CDS-not-defined and lncRNA isoforms flip most** (`r round(100 * by_type$cutoff_flip[by_type$type == "retained_intron"], 1)`%, `r round(100 * by_type$cutoff_flip[by_type$type == "protein_coding_CDS_not_defined"], 1)`% and `r round(100 * by_type$cutoff_flip[by_type$type == "lncRNA"], 1)`%): they have fewer reads and their InfRV sits near the cutoff, where a noisier estimate decides the call.
- **lncRNA trees are the least stable**: `r round(100 * by_type$tree_changed[by_type$type == "lncRNA"], 1)`% of lncRNA isoforms are in a tree whose transcripts change between 30 and 100 draws, against `r round(100 * by_type$tree_changed[by_type$type == "protein_coding"], 1)`% of protein-coding ones.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
by_type |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c("cutoff_flip", "tree_changed"), names_to = "measure", values_to = "share") |>
  mutate(
    type = factor(type_labels[type], levels = type_labels),
    measure = c(cutoff_flip = "cutoff flip, 30 vs 30 draws", tree_changed = "tree changed, 30 vs 100 draws")[measure]
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = type, y = share)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#4C72B0") +
  facet_wrap(vars(measure)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Isoforms") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

The tree changes matter for the isoforms that a cut of the trees would group, the uncertain ones; for lncRNAs they are as frequent among those:

```{r}
stability("tree_uncertainty") |>
  filter(type %in% c("protein_coding", "retained_intron", "lncRNA"))
```

## What the features say

The median InfRV across the levels of each feature, for all isoforms and within the three largest types:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 9
bins <- stability("feature_bins")
bins |>
  filter(
    feature %in% c("reads", "unique_fraction", "isoforms_in_gene", "tx_length", "closest_bp", "unique_bp", "n_exons", "gc"),
    type %in% c("all", "protein_coding", "retained_intron", "lncRNA")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    type = factor(type_labels[type], levels = type_labels),
    level = reorder(level, level_order)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = level, y = median_inf_rv, colour = type, group = type)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(vars(feature), scales = "free_x", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Median InfRV (log scale)", colour = NULL, caption = "Dashed: the cutoff of add_uncertainty()") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1), legend.position = "top")
```

- **Fragments of its own decide whether an isoform is determined.** The median InfRV falls from about 6 for isoforms without a unique fragment to 0.02 for those with most fragments unique, within every type.
- **Sequence identity to siblings works the same way**: isoforms that differ from their closest sibling by few bases, or that have few exonic bases of their own, are the most uncertain.
- **More isoforms in the gene, more uncertainty**: from 0.05 for genes with one isoform to about 4 for genes with more than 30.
- **Uncertainty is not a problem of low counts.** The InfRV rises with the number of reads up to a thousand reads: an ambiguous isoform stays ambiguous however deep it is sequenced, plausibly because the variance that assignment adds grows with the reads that have to be assigned. Length works the same way for protein-coding isoforms, which share more exons as they grow.
- **GC content hardly matters** once the rest is known.

The cutoff flips follow a different pattern: they are rare where the InfRV is far from the cutoff in either direction and frequent near it.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
bins |>
  filter(feature %in% c("unique_fraction", "reads"), type %in% c("all", "protein_coding", "retained_intron", "lncRNA")) |>
  mutate(type = factor(type_labels[type], levels = type_labels), level = reorder(level, level_order)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = level, y = cutoff_flip, fill = type)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  facet_wrap(vars(feature), scales = "free_x") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Cutoff flips, 30 vs 30 draws", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Isoforms with some but few unique fragments (5% to 25%) flip most, and low-count isoforms flip more than well-covered ones: these are the isoforms whose call depends on the replicates, and for which more draws help.

### Splice sites

NAGNAG acceptors, where two isoforms differ by three bases at an acceptor, are a classical hard case for read assignment.

```{r}
bins |>
  filter(feature %in% c("nagnag", "near_acceptor", "near_donor", "contained", "mane"), type %in% c("all", "protein_coding")) |>
  select(feature, type, level, isoforms, median_inf_rv, cutoff_flip, tree_changed)
```

Isoforms with a NAGNAG or a nearby alternative acceptor or donor are more uncertain, but the model below attributes almost none of that to the splice sites themselves once the unique fragments are known: a three-base difference leaves the isoform with very few fragments of its own, and that is what the replicates register.
MANE Select isoforms are less uncertain than the other protein-coding isoforms of their genes, and closer to the cutoff, so they flip more often.

## Separating the factors

The features are correlated (long isoforms have more exons; genes with many isoforms have isoforms with few unique bases), so their individual effects come from models that include them all, with the continuous features standardised.
The share of the explained deviance of each feature:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
importance <- stability("importance")
importance |>
  mutate(
    outcome = c(
      log_inf_rv = "InfRV (log)",
      log_rv_disagreement = "InfRV disagreement, 30 vs 30",
      tree_changed = "tree changed, 30 vs 100"
    )[outcome],
    term = reorder(term, share)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = share, y = term)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#4C72B0") +
  facet_wrap(vars(outcome), nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Share of explained deviance", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
stability("model_fit")
```

- **How uncertain an isoform is** is well explained (R² `r stability("model_fit")$r_squared[1]`): the unique fragments, the reads, the MANE tag, the length and the distance to the closest sibling carry most of it.
- **How much two sets of 30 draws disagree** is mostly not explained by any feature (R² `r stability("model_fit")$r_squared[2]`): it is sampling noise of the draws, which only more draws reduce. The disagreement on the log scale is largest for the best-determined isoforms, whose InfRV is close to zero; on the decisions that matter (the cutoff) the flips above are the better summary.
- **Whether the tree changes** depends mostly on the transcript type and on the number of isoforms of the gene: lncRNA loci and genes with many isoforms have the least stable trees.

The direction of each effect:

```{r}
stability("model_terms") |>
  filter(!grepl("^type|Intercept", term)) |>
  select(outcome, term, estimate, p_value) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = outcome, values_from = c(estimate, p_value))
```

## How to read the uncertainty of an isoform

- **A high InfRV means an isoform shares its reads, not that it has few.** Look at `unique_fraction` in `tx_uncertainty()`: an isoform with almost no fragment of its own will stay uncertain at any depth, and the honest unit for it is a group (`collapse_groups`, Terminus or TreeTerminus).
- **Calls near the cutoff are the fragile ones.** Isoforms with a few unique fragments, few reads, retained introns, lncRNAs and transcripts without a defined CDS are where 30 draws can tip the call; for those, 100 draws make the classes more stable (`salmon_quant(num_gibbs = 100)`).
- **TreeTerminus on lncRNA-rich questions needs more draws.** About half of the lncRNA trees change between 30 and 100 draws, also for uncertain isoforms.
- **Splice-site structure acts through the reads.** NAGNAG and nearby alternative splice sites make isoforms hard to separate because they leave them without unique fragments; `unique_fraction` already measures that, so there is no need to correct for it separately.
- **The MANE isoform is the easiest isoform of a coding gene to quantify**, which also makes it the most common reference when the other isoforms are uncertain.

## Cautions

The measures come from three samples of one experiment, quantified with one tool (Salmon 2.8.0) on 12 million read pairs; deeper libraries may move isoforms relative to the cutoff (not tested here), and other quantifiers distribute ambiguous reads differently.
The cutoff flips compare two halves of one Salmon run, a clean comparison of 30 draws with 30 draws; the tree changes compare two separate Salmon runs, so they mix the effect of the number of draws with the randomness of an independent run.
The features describe the annotation; isoforms absent from it, and reads from them, are outside this picture.
